formulaCard.title: Sampling Methods Summary
notes: Random, stratified, and cluster sampling are preferred when designed well.
Convenience and self‑selected samples are usually biased.

rows.2: Medium — may align with a hidden pattern
Medium — depends on how clusters are formed

explanation: A [[kw:random sample]] gives every member of the population an equal chance of being selected. It is the gold standard.
A [[kw:self‑selected sample]] lets volunteers choose to participate. Often biased because those with strong opinions respond.
A [[kw:systematic sample]] uses a rule (e.g., every 10th person) to select members. Quick and easy, but may miss patterns.
A [[kw:stratified sample]] splits the population into similar groups (strata) and randomly selects some from each. Ensures all groups are represented.
A [[kw:cluster sample]] splits the population into clusters, then randomly selects entire clusters to study. Useful when the population is spread out.
A [[kw:convenience sample]] selects people who are easy to reach. It's the weakest method because it often misrepresents the population.

blocks.title: Types of Samples

discoveryHook.scenario: Imagine you want to find out the average number of hours students at your school spend on homework. You could ask every student (a census), but that takes forever! Sampling lets you ask a smaller group — but how you pick that group is crucial. Different sampling methods can give very different results.

notes: Random sampling is the best defense against bias.
Always ask: who is left out of this sample?

rows.0: Dog park survey about off‑leash area (80 dog owners at park)

explanation: [[kw:Bias]] is a systematic error that makes a sample not representative of the population.
An [[kw:unbiased sample]] fairly represents the whole population. A [[kw:biased sample]] overrepresents or underrepresents some part of the population.
Common sources of bias: using a convenience sample, allowing self‑selection, or using a sampling frame that misses part of the population.
To reduce bias, use a random sampling method, ensure a high response rate, and make sure the sample size is large enough.

discoveryHook.scenario: If you ask only people at a gym how often they exercise, you'll probably get a much higher average than the true population. That's bias — the sample overrepresents fitness enthusiasts. Recognizing bias helps you avoid drawing wrong conclusions.

confusionCorner.title: Random ≠ Perfectly Representative
confusionCorner.body: A random sample can still produce unusual results by chance, especially if the sample size is small. However, it's the best method we have to minimize bias. [[imp:Random doesn't mean the sample exactly matches the population; it means the selection process is fair.]]

explanation: An [[kw:experiment]] imposes a treatment on individuals to measure the effect. It can establish cause‑and‑effect.
An [[kw:observational study]] observes and measures variables without controlling the environment. It shows association, not necessarily causation.
A [[kw:survey]] asks every member of a sample one or more questions. Surveys rely on self‑reported data.
A [[kw:simulation]] uses a model (often computer‑based) to reproduce conditions of a process. It's used when real‑world experiments are impractical or dangerous.

notes: Observational studies and surveys reveal correlation or patterns.

confusionCorner.title: Experiment vs. Observational Study
confusionCorner.body: The key difference: experiments [[imp:apply a treatment]] to some individuals. Observational studies just watch. Because of this, only experiments can prove that one thing causes another.

discoveryHook.scenario: You can collect data in many ways: you could run a controlled experiment (like testing a new medicine), observe without interfering (watching animals in the wild), ask people directly (a survey), or even use a computer simulation to predict the spread of a virus. Choosing the right method is the first step in any statistical study.

confusionCorner.title: Sensitive Topics Need Anonymity
confusionCorner.body: Questions about illegal behavior, health, or income may get dishonest answers if people fear judgment. Offering [[imp:anonymity]] and neutral wording helps. A survey on paper in a box is better than a face‑to‑face interview for sensitive topics.

discoveryHook.scenario: The way a question is worded can push people toward a certain answer. 'Do you support wasteful spending on a new stadium?' is very different from 'Do you support building a stadium to bring jobs and entertainment?' Neutral wording is essential for honest data.

examples.prompt: A police officer asks mall visitors, 'Do you wear your seat belt regularly?' Explain why this may be biased.
examples.title: Example A – Spotting Bias
steps: People may not want to admit to a police officer that they don't wear a seat belt.
The authority figure creates pressure to give a 'good' answer.
This introduces [[kw:social desirability bias]] — respondents give the answer they think is expected, not necessarily the truth.

Explain to a partner: Why is asking about two different things in one question a problem? How would you split it into two unbiased questions?
steps: It asks about budget cuts and tax cuts at the same time — a person might agree with one but not the other.
This is a [[kw:double‑barreled question]].
Fix: Ask two separate questions: (1) 'Do you support cutting the budget?' (2) 'Do you support lowering taxes?'
examples.title: Example B – Fixing a Double‑Barreled Question
examples.prompt: Explain why 'Do you think the budget should be cut and taxes should be lowered?' is a bad question. How can you fix it?
Is 'Don't you agree that our city needs more parks?' a biased question? If so, rewrite it.
steps: Yes, it's leading — 'Don't you agree' pushes the respondent toward 'yes'.
It also assumes the city needs more parks without evidence.
Unbiased version: 'Do you think the number of parks in our city is too many, too few, or about right?'
examples.title: Example C – Leading Question

teacherCues: Write a biased question: 'Don't you agree that our school should have longer recess?' Ask students what's wrong.
Show how to rewrite it neutrally: 'Do you think the length of recess should be increased, decreased, or stay the same?'

explanation: A [[kw:biased question]] is worded in a way that encourages a particular response or makes it hard to answer truthfully.
Common flaws: leading language ('Don't you think...'), emotionally charged words ('dangerous', 'healthy'), double‑barreled questions (asking two things at once), or questions that make assumptions.
To write an [[imp:unbiased question]], use neutral language, avoid assumptions, and make sure all possible answers are covered.

discoveryHook.scenario: You're asked to conduct a statistical study. Where do you start? The Data Collection Blueprint walks you through identifying your goal, picking a fair sampling method, choosing how to collect data, and writing unbiased questions — so your conclusions are trustworthy!

blocks.title: Blueprint Aid – Designing a Data Collection Plan

rows.1: What is the population? What do I want to know?
What sampling method? How big a sample?
Is the sample fair? Are questions neutral?

explanation: 1. [[imp:Understand]] – Define the population, the variable of interest, and the goal. Do you need to compare groups (experiment) or just describe (survey/observational)?
2. [[imp:Plan the Sample]] – Choose a sampling method that minimizes bias. Random, stratified, or cluster is preferred. Decide on the sample size.
3. [[imp:Choose a Data Collection Method]] – Experiment, observational study, survey, or simulation. Write clear, unbiased questions if surveying.
4. [[imp:Check for Bias]] – Review the sampling method and questions for potential bias. Adjust as needed to ensure representativeness and honest responses.

formulaCard.title: Study Design Blueprint
notes: A well‑designed study follows these steps in order.
Pilot testing questions on a few people can reveal hidden bias.

steps: Understand: Population = all 1200 students. Variable = hours of sleep. Goal: estimate the mean.
Plan the sample: Use a stratified random sample — select 5 students randomly from each grade to ensure representation. Total sample size = 4 grades × 5 = 20 (or larger if possible).
Choose method: Survey. Ask a clear, unbiased question: 'On average, how many hours of sleep do you get per school night?' Provide ranges if needed.
Check for bias: The sample is small but stratified. The question is neutral. Consider anonymity to get honest answers.

steps: Understand: Population = students in a particular class. Variable = test score. Want to compare app users vs. non‑users.
